proposals.before: Lady of the District Qu bore the Prince of Hengyang, Jun;
proposals.after: Honorable Lady Qu bore the Prince of Hengyang, Jun;
proposals.reason: 區 is the surname Qu and 貴人 is the inner-palace rank Honorable Lady, not a lady of a district.

proposals.before: Prince Xian of Linchuan, Ying, styled Xuangguang, was the founding emperor's third son.
proposals.after: Prince Xian of Linchuan, Ying, styled Xuanguang, was the founding emperor's third son.
proposals.reason: 宣光 is Xuanguang; Xuangguang is a misspelling of the courtesy name.

proposals.before: Prince Xian of Linchuan Ying, styled Xuangguang, was the founding emperor's third son.
proposals.after: Prince Xian of Linchuan Ying, styled Xuanguang, was the founding emperor's third son.
proposals.reason: 宣光 is Xuanguang; the literal field repeats the same misspelling of the courtesy name.

proposals.before: When the affair was settled, he was made adviser to the central army, attendant gentleman, aide to the state, general of assisting the state, and grand administrator of Huainan and Xuancheng — both posts he declined.
proposals.after: When the affair was settled, he was made adviser to the central army, attendant gentleman, and general of assisting the state, and grand administrator of Huainan and Xuancheng — none of which he accepted.
proposals.reason: 並不拜 means he accepted none of the listed appointments, not only two prefect posts; 輔國將軍 is one title, not a separate aide plus general.

proposals.before: In year five he was made Grand Mentor with ceremony equal to the Three Dukes at his present rank.
proposals.after: In year five, at his present rank, he was granted a headquarters with ceremonial equality to the Three Dukes.
proposals.reason: 開府儀同三司 is not Grand Mentor (太傅); it is the privilege of opening a headquarters with Three-Dukes ceremony.

proposals.before: In year five he was made Grand Mentor with the same title at his present rank.
proposals.after: In year five, at his present rank, he was granted a headquarters with ceremonial equality to the Three Dukes.
proposals.reason: Literal English also renders 開府儀同三司 as Grand Mentor.

proposals.before: The emperor was furious and by his own hand issued an edict a beating with the staff.
proposals.after: The emperor was furious and by his own hand issued an edict ordering a beating with the staff.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic sentence is ungrammatical and obscures 手詔賜杖.

proposals.before: The emperor was greatly angered and by hand-edict granted him a beating staff.
proposals.after: The emperor was greatly angered and by handwritten edict granted him a beating with the staff.
proposals.reason: 賜杖 is a beating with the staff, not the gift of a staff.

proposals.before: Contemporaries judged Emperor Wu better than Cao Pi and less than Liu Zhuang of Han Ming.
proposals.after: Contemporaries judged Emperor Wu better than Emperor Wen of Wei and less than Emperor Ming of Han.
proposals.reason: 魏文 and 漢明 are imperial posthumous titles, not the fused phrase Liu Zhuang of Han Ming.

proposals.before: At his present rank he was posthumously made Grand Mentor with Three-Dukes ceremony.
proposals.after: At his present rank he was posthumously granted a headquarters with ceremonial equality to the Three Dukes.
proposals.reason: Same mistranslation of 開府儀同三司 as Grand Mentor.

proposals.before: At his present rank he was posthumously made Grand Mentor with ceremony equal to the Three Dukes.
proposals.after: At his present rank he was posthumously granted a headquarters with ceremonial equality to the Three Dukes.
proposals.reason: Same mistranslation of 開府儀同三司 as Grand Mentor.

proposals.before: The founding emperor often said: "This is our house's Prince of Ren."
proposals.after: The founding emperor often said: "This is our house's Prince of Rencheng."
proposals.reason: 任城 is Rencheng; Prince of Ren truncates the fief name.

proposals.before: The founding emperor often said: "This is my family's Prince of Ren."
proposals.after: The founding emperor often said: "This is my family's Prince of Rencheng."
proposals.reason: 任城 is Rencheng; Prince of Ren truncates the fief name.

proposals.before: When Emperor Wu ascended Ye was advanced to General of the Left and entered as director of the secretariat, rank unchanged.
proposals.after: When Emperor Wu ascended, Ye was advanced to General of the Left and entered as director of the secretariat, rank unchanged.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic English fuses the accession clause with Ye, omitting the required comma/subject break after ascended.

proposals.before: Soon he was transferred former general and grand minister of rituals, repeatedly thwarted in his aims.
proposals.after: Soon he was transferred to Front General and grand minister of rituals, repeatedly thwarted in his aims.
proposals.reason: 前將軍 is Front General, not “former general”; the literal English drops the office sense.

proposals.before: On his deathbed the Shizu's final edict made Ye Defender General and Grand Mentor with Three-Dukes ceremony, with martial pipes and drums.
proposals.after: On his deathbed the Shizu's final edict made Ye General of the Guards and granted him an office with ceremonial equal to the Three Dukes, with martial pipes and drums.
proposals.reason: 衛將軍 is General of the Guards, not Defender General (護軍), and 開府儀同三司 is not Grand Mentor.

proposals.before: In year four he went out bearer of credentials, commander of Jinxu affairs in Jiang and Yu, Southern Central Army General, and governor of Jiang.
proposals.after: In year four he went out bearer of credentials, commander of Jinxi affairs in Jiang and Yu, Southern Central Army General, and governor of Jiang.
proposals.reason: 晉熙 is Jinxi; the literal spelling Jinxu is a corruption.

proposals.before: In Yanxing year one he was posthumously advanced to Grand Mentor, attendant and Rapid Cavalry unchanged.
proposals.after: In Yanxing year one he was advanced to Minister of Education, with attendant and Rapid Cavalry unchanged.
proposals.reason: Chinese 進位司徒 is a living promotion to Situ, not a posthumous gift, and 司徒 is not Grand Mentor (太傅).

proposals.before: In the first year of Yanxing he was posthumously advanced to Grand Mentor, attendant and Rapid Cavalry as before.
proposals.after: In the first year of Yanxing he was advanced to Minister of Education, with attendant and Rapid Cavalry as before.
proposals.reason: Chinese 進位司徒 is advancement to Situ while alive; 司徒 is not Grand Mentor, and there is no 追.

proposals.before: When the Prince of Poyang was killed, Shuo was made general of the central army and Grand Mentor with Three-Dukes ceremony.
proposals.after: When the Prince of Poyang was killed, Shuo was made General of the Central Army and granted open office with ceremony equal to the Three Dukes.
proposals.reason: 開府儀同三司 is the Three-Dukes ceremonial privilege, not Grand Mentor (太傅).

proposals.before: When Prince of Poyang was killed, Shuo was moved general of the central army and Grand Mentor with Three-Dukes ceremony.
proposals.after: When Prince of Poyang was killed, Shuo was moved General of the Central Army and granted open office with ceremony equal to the Three Dukes.
proposals.reason: Literal likewise renders 開府儀同三司 as Grand Mentor, which is the wrong office.

proposals.before: He was first enfeoffed Prince of Guangxing; later the fief moved to Suizhou and the title changed.
proposals.after: He was first enfeoffed Prince of Guangxing; later the fief's name followed the commandery's change of name.
proposals.reason: 后國隨郡改名 means the title followed a commandery rename, not a move to Suizhou.

proposals.before: He was first enfeoffed Prince of Guangxing; later the state followed Suizhou and the name was changed.
proposals.after: He was first enfeoffed Prince of Guangxing; later the state followed the commandery and the name was changed.
proposals.reason: 隨郡 is 'followed the commandery', not the place-name Suizhou.

proposals.before: Prince of Hedong, Xuan, styled Xuanyi, was the founding emperor's nineteenth son.
proposals.after: Prince of Hedong, Xuan, styled Xuanyin, was the founding emperor's nineteenth son.
proposals.reason: Courtesy name 宣胤 is Xuanyin, not Xuanyi.

proposals.before: Prince of Hedong Xuan, styled Xuanyi, was the founding emperor's nineteenth son.
proposals.after: Prince of Hedong Xuan, styled Xuanyin, was the founding emperor's nineteenth son.
proposals.reason: Courtesy name 宣胤 is Xuanyin, not Xuanyi.

proposals.before: When the High Emperor executed the princes, because Xuan was young and weak in talent he was not harmed.
proposals.after: When Gaozong executed the princes, because Xuan was young and weak in talent he was not harmed.
proposals.reason: 高宗 is temple name Gaozong (Emperor Ming), not High Emperor.

decisions.reason: 區貴人 is surname Qu plus the inner-palace rank 貴人; neighboring consorts are likewise named by rank (修容, 太妃, 淑妃, 美人), not as a lady of a district.
字宣光 is the courtesy name Xuanguang; Xuangguang is a misspelling.
The same courtesy name 宣光 must be Xuanguang in the literal field as well.

decisions.after: When the affair was settled, he was made adviser to the central army, attendant gentleman, general of assisting the state, and grand administrator of Huainan and Xuancheng — none of which he accepted.
decisions.reason: 並不拜 covers every listed appointment, and 輔國將軍 is a single title, not an extra 'aide to the state'; the proposed list still inserts a superfluous 'and' before that generalship.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 除中軍諮議、從事中郎、輔國將軍、淮南宣城二郡太守，並不拜

decisions.reason: 即本號開府儀同三司 is the privilege of opening a headquarters with Three-Dukes ceremony at his existing rank, not appointment as Grand Mentor (太傅).
The literal field likewise misrenders 開府儀同三司 as Grand Mentor; 即本號 keeps his present title while granting that privilege.
手詔賜杖 is an imperial handwritten edict ordering a staff beating; the original English is ungrammatical and drops the verb of command.
賜杖 is punishment by beating with the staff, not the conferral of a staff as an object.
The Chinese compares 世祖 with 魏文 and 漢明, the posthumous titles of Wei Wendi and Han Mingdi; 'Cao Pi' and 'Liu Zhuang of Han Ming' invent personal names and garble 漢明.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 優於魏文， 減于漢明

decisions.reason: 贈開府儀同三司 is a posthumous grant of headquarters with Three-Dukes ceremony, not Grand Mentor.
The literal field repeats the same false Grand Mentor rendering of 開府儀同三司.
任城 is the fief Rencheng; 'Prince of Ren' truncates the place-name in 此我家任城也.
The literal quotation likewise needs the full fief name Rencheng for 任城.
世祖即位，進號… has a clause break after the accession; without the comma, 'ascended Ye' garden-paths Ye as the object of accession.
前將軍 is the office Front General, not a 'former' general.

decisions.after: On his deathbed the Shizu's final edict made Ye General of the Guards and granted him a headquarters with ceremonial equality to the Three Dukes, with martial pipes and drums.
decisions.reason: 衛將軍 is General of the Guards, not Defender General (護軍), and 開府儀同三司 is not Grand Mentor; the proposed 'an office with ceremonial equal' is still awkward.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 遺詔為衛將軍，開府儀同三司

decisions.reason: 晉熙 is Jinxi; Jinxu is a corrupted romanization.
進位司徒 is a living advancement to Situ (Minister of Education); the text has neither 追/贈 nor 太傅, and the following narrative still shows him alive.
The literal field makes the same two errors: there is no posthumous marker, and 司徒 is not Grand Mentor.
鑠遷中軍將軍，開府儀同三司 grants central-army generalship plus the Three-Dukes ceremonial privilege, not Grand Mentor.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 遷中軍將軍，開府儀同三司

decisions.reason: The literal field likewise misidentifies 開府儀同三司 as Grand Mentor.
后國隨郡改名 means the princely title followed the commandery's rename (廣興 to 始興), not a transfer to Suizhou.
隨郡 is 'followed the commandery', not the toponym Suizhou.
字宣胤 is Xuanyin; 胤 is yin, not yi.
The literal courtesy name must also be Xuanyin for 宣胤.
高宗 is the temple name Gaozong; High Emperor would render 高帝, a different person.
